title: Benchmarks: writing them, reading the result and not fooling yourself

videos.script: A test says whether the code is right. A benchmark says how long it takes, and how much memory it asks for. {{writing}} You write two, in the same test files, and run them with go test. The loop that is timed is b.Loop. Everything before it is setup, and is left out. {{reading}} Then the columns: time per round, bytes, allocations. Five runs of the same code differ by a few percent. That spread is the noise, and a smaller change has not been measured. {{candidate}} You try a faster version of the counting function. The allocations fall by exactly two hundred and fifty six, and the time by about a tenth. Then you decide it is not worth its twenty lines, and put the old one back. {{fooling}} Last, three ways a benchmark lies. The compiler deletes the work, the setup gets timed, or the machine is busy. {{close}} Lesson 30 measures something else: how much of the code the tests reach.
